big_idea: We compare CAPACITY by pouring. Holds more, holds less, or same.
learning_intention: We are learning to compare how much things hold.
student_learning_goal: I can compare how much things hold.
success_criteria: I can pour from one container to another to compare.
I can say which holds more or holds less.
I can say when two containers hold the SAME amount.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Max and Tess — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Anchor chart 'Holds More / Holds Less / Same'
3 real cups of different sizes (small, medium, large)
A bag of dried beans or rice for pouring
Lesson 3 capacity tracker — provided in assessment_suite stage

minds_on.hook: Max: This big cup is full of beans. Will all the beans fit in this small cup? Let's see!
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Max + Tess puppets. 'Yesterday we compared MASS. Today we compare CAPACITY — HOW MUCH it HOLDS.'

Write HOLDS MORE, HOLDS LESS, SAME on chart. 'More = bigger amount. Less = smaller amount. Same = equal.'

Demonstrate pouring. Big cup full of beans. 'Pour into this small cup. Watch — OVERFLOWS! Small cup holds LESS. Big cup holds MORE.'

Same: two same-size cups. Pour one into the other. 'Fit perfectly. SAME capacity.'

The SURPRISE: tall thin tube vs wide short bowl. 'Which holds more? Pour to find out.' Bowl wins! 'TALLER is NOT always MORE. POUR is the test.'

Max's RULE: 'LINE IT UP — COMPARE — NAME IT!' For capacity: line them up by pouring, compare which overflows, name HOLDS MORE or HOLDS LESS.

Class refrain. Class chants 3x with claps: 'LINE IT UP — COMPARE — NAME IT! That's how Max measures!'

'Today we POUR and COMPARE cups.'
student_actions: Watch Max pour beans between cups.

steps.instruction: Whole group: pour and compare 4 pairs of containers. (a) bowl vs thimble. (b) juice box vs mug. (c) two same-size cups. (d) water bottle vs juice box.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say: 'Predict first. Then pour. Which holds more?'

steps.instruction: Three stations. Station A: Cup Sort — sort 12 cup cards by size into 3 piles (small / medium / large). Station B: Pour and Compare — pair pours beans between 4 real cups and records more/less. Station C: Find Same — pair finds 3 pairs of same-capacity containers.
Stretch challenge at Station B: order 5 cups from smallest to largest capacity by pouring.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say: 'Stretch: order 5 from smallest capacity to largest.'

steps.instruction: Discuss the pour rule. 'POUR from one to the other. Watch — does it overflow, fit perfectly, or leave room?'
steps.teacher_prompt: Demonstrate again with two cups, one bigger.

steps.instruction: Circulate to record formative evidence on the capacity tracker.
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Ask 'Which holds more? Show me by pouring.' Mark the tracker.

differentiation.for_emerging: Stay at Station A. Just sort by visible size (no pouring).
differentiation.for_extending: Stretch at Station B: order 5 cups by capacity using pour-tests only.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Provide a sentence frame: 'This holds ___ than that.'
differentiation.for_movement_learners: NO-PAPER, NO-WATER PATH: pour DRY rice or beans (or paper-clip / pebble counts as a stand-in 'unit'). No sand/water table required. Children kneel on the floor with two paper plates as 'pans'; pour from cup A onto plate then into cup B; if the pile overflows cup B, cup B holds LESS. Whole lesson can run with only classroom cups, beans, and bodies — no purchased materials.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: pours carefully; says holds more/less correctly; recognizes 'same capacity'.

discussion_prompts: How do you compare two cups? (POUR — don't eyeball.)
Tall and thin vs short and wide — which always wins? (Neither — POUR is the test.)
consolidation.exit_routine: Refrain chant 3x. Then each child completes the sentence frame: 'My ___ HOLDS MORE than my ___' (or HOLDS LESS / SAME). Sticky-note one capacity comparison and post.

assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Lesson 3 captures A10.2 mastery for capacity.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child says TALLER means HOLDS MORE — repairing the height-capacity conflation at K (Piaget, 1969 conservation-of-liquid; Sarama & Clements, 2009)
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On A10.2 capacity comparison, the most-documented K trap is the height-capacity conflation: child says the TALLER container must hold more. This is the classic Piagetian conservation-of-liquid trap: poured into a tall thin tube, water now 'holds more' than it did in the wide short cup it came from.

Piaget (1969) showed that pre-conservation children attend to a single salient dimension — usually height — and ignore the compensating reduction in width. The K child watches water rise in the thin tube and concludes the amount itself increased. Conservation of liquid is a Grade 1-2 achievement; the K target is more modest: establish that POURING is the empirical test for capacity, regardless of which container 'looks bigger'. Sarama & Clements (2009) place this perceptual-to-empirical handoff at the start of the K capacity trajectory: physical pour with surprise pairs (wide-short vs tall-thin) generates the cognitive friction that begins to dislodge the height = amount fusion.

Why this matters: capacity depends on VOLUME, not just height. Without the surprise pair, children leave K with their height-capacity fusion intact and arrive in Grade 1 still mis-reading liquid measure.

The walkthrough covers when a child equates height with capacity.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at Station B. Child has a tall thin tube and a wide short bowl. Says 'tube holds more, it's taller'.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch. 'You said the tube holds more. Let's POUR and check.'

Fill the tube with beans. Pour into the bowl. The tube empties but the bowl is only half-full. 'See — the bowl can take MORE. So the BOWL holds more.'

Walk through. 'Max says — LINE IT UP by pouring. COMPARE which overflows. NAME IT.'

Generalise. 'Wide short bowls can hold a lot. Tall thin tubes can hold less than they look. POUR is the test.'

Now verify in reverse: fill the bowl, pour into the tube. The tube overflows.

If still judging by height: provide surprise pairs (wide bowl + tall tube). Force the POUR behaviour.

Long-term recovery: every capacity comparison pours first, judges second.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Says taller = holds more without pouring; height-amount fused.
(Mid) Pours with prompts, surprised by results.
(Strong) Pours first, names which holds more independently.
(Stretched) Predicts capacity before pouring AND can rank 4 containers; can articulate 'thin and tall can hold less than wide and short'.
common_misconceptions: Taller = holds more. (Repair: pour to compare, height alone doesn't decide capacity.)
Wider = holds more. (Repair: width alone doesn't either; only POURING settles it.)
Same shape = same capacity. (Repair: shape and capacity are different — verify by pour in BOTH directions.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child still uses height after one surprise pair: line up FOUR pre-staged surprise pairs (wide bowl vs tall tube, mug vs measuring cylinder, ramekin vs tall glass, bowl vs juice box); make the child predict, then pour, then mark the result; accumulating counter-evidence pries the height-capacity fusion apart.

DIAGNOSTIC B — child pours one direction only and asserts the result is final ('overflowed, so the FIRST one holds more'): drill the TWO-WAY pour: 'now reverse — fill the OTHER one and pour back'; only when both directions agree does the answer count.

DIAGNOSTIC C — child pours from a WIDE container into a NARROW one and panics at the rising column ('it grew!'): mark the bean line on the outside of the wide container before pouring; show that the bean COUNT didn't change, only the COLUMN shape changed; end-of-pour: 'same beans, different look — same capacity'.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of A10.2 capacity comparison.

parts_outline.task: Circle the container that holds more in 5 pairs.
Order 4 cups from smallest to largest capacity.
Draw 2 things in your kitchen. Circle the one that holds more.
